This comment is made as I read the article.

Astrology, for instance, is falsifiable — indeed, it has been falsified ad nauseam — and yet it isn’t science.

Since it has been falsified, we no longer treat it as true. How can a professor be this dumb? No one is arguing that as long as something is falsifiable it is a good scientific theory. If it is falsifiable and is falsified, then it isn't true. This isn't hard to comprehend. Falsification is still the best method for dealing with what is scientific or not.

Bayesianism allows for the fact that modern scientific theories typically make claims far beyond what can be directly observed — no one has ever seen an atom — and so today’s theories often resist a falsified-unfalsified dichotomy

The ability to be falsified and then proceed to not be falsified does not stand in the way of a probabilistic method of creating the model. The probability of correctness is always based on empirical data, which no one can dispute. When you are fitting an equation to data, you will always need to do a statistical analysis of it to determine certain parameters that tell you if it is a good fit. Each field requires their own parameters to be met for the model to be correct. No where does science allow non-empirical and subjective evidence, which is what this article will present. Those who wish to keep science as it is, the same science that developed radios, atomic bombs, airplanes, and computers, should shun this subjective evidence, as it gets in the way of learning what reality is actually about. The science that flew men to the moon and safely back again depends on non-biased evidence, which subjective evidence cannot rid itself of. Science - it works, bitches. But only if it remains pure can it hope to remain the greatest achievement in human thinking.

First, there appears to be only one version of string theory capable of achieving unification in a consistent way (though it has many different mathematical representations); furthermore, no other “theory of everything” capable of unifying all the fundamental forces has been found, despite immense effort.

Just because your mind can't conceive of another theory, doesn't mean there isn't another one. The inability to develop something at this moment in time is not an argument that one cannot be developed later.

Second, string theory grew out of the Standard Model — the accepted, empirically validated theory incorporating all known fundamental particles and forces (apart from gravity) in a single mathematical structure — and the Standard Model also had no alternatives during its formative years. This “meta-inductive” argument, as Dawid calls it, buttresses the no-alternatives argument by showing that it has worked before in similar contexts, countering the possibility that physicists simply aren’t clever enough to find the alternatives that exist.

Just because you cannot think of a different theory, doesn't mean one doesn't exist. By 'meta-inductive' I assume he means mathematical induction. Inductive proofs require two things to be true for the argument to be true. First, there must be a base case. Second, logic must be shown that if the previous is true, then the next is true. For those who are unfamiliar with this concept, I'll prove I can climb a ladder. First, I can reach the first rung of the ladder. Second, if I am at one rung of the ladder, I can reach the next rung of the ladder. Therefore, I can climb the ladder, even if the ladder is infinitely long. This is nice, since I can prove things that go on without end. To those who can read between the lines, you can already see where the Dawid's argument is lacking. Dawid never proves the inductive step, or the step that shows that the next is true, if the previous is. He argues that the base case being true bolsters his claim in some way. Anyone who has dabbled in computer science knows this is not true. For thos who are sitting at home, let me show you a case :

Let me argue that the Fibonacci sequence starts at 1 and then repeats itself. The Fibonacci sequence is:

1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, ...

The base case stands. Using Dawid's logic, this increases the probability that the entire argument is true. As you can see, the Fibonacci sequence is not a sequence of ones. Meeting the base case is no indicator of satisfying the inductive step.

Also, just because physicists have been right in a hypothesis beforehand does not mean that they always do this. Physicists thought they had resolved light to being only a wave, but Einstein's, Milikan's and Planck's work showed that the wave-particle duality was the best model. They were completely wrong on the wave theory of light and can be wrong again.

“But acknowledging that non-empirical confirmation is part of science, and has been part of science for quite some time, provides a better basis for having that discussion than pretending that it wasn’t there, and only implicitly using it, and then saying I haven’t done it. Once it’s out in the open, one can discuss the pros and cons of those arguments within a specific context.”

I have never heard of confirmation of a scientific theory before empirical evidence for it existed. Someone would have to show that for me to believe it.

Dawid is a philosopher, not a scientist. He should stick to that, as he doesn't understand that science is an empirical study of nature.

Sabine Hossenfelder makes a terrific argument. Assuming that our guesses are correct about the unknown should be left to theologians. Neil DeGrasse Tyson once said something along the lines of, "'if you throw your hands up and say 'god did it', then you are no longer useful in the lab." The same should be said about anyone who decides that they have figured everything out and can't provide empirical evidence.

Overall, I don't really care about how Dawid's criteria are being proposed to be used by Grow. How scientists rank their favorite pet theories won't effect how science operates.
